title: Chapter Twenty-Two: What It Costs to Hold

blocks.c: Chapter Twenty-Two: What It Costs to Hold
Tamsin Roake did not go deaf all at once, which everyone had assumed she had.

What she had lost, the surgeon at Antrell said, was the high end and most of the middle, permanently and comprehensively, on both sides. She could hear a shout as a kind of pressure. She could hear Mother, the deepest bell but one, as a sensation in the chest. She could not hear a voice, or a bell tail, or her own footsteps, and never would again.
She was fifty-nine years old and had been the best ear on the run for thirty of them.

The Company offered her a pension at two thirds and a cottage at Antrell with a view of the ridge, and it was, Halloway said, a genuinely decent offer by the standards of an institution that had written nil in a book for eleven years.
Roake read the letter twice and wrote four words on her slate and turned it round.
I am not finished.

Sol went with her to the surgeon and stood in the corridor afterwards and cried in the ugly, undignified, hiccuping way she had not done since she was eleven, and Roake waited it out, and then wrote on the slate she now carried everywhere:
Stop that. I can still feel a round through the deck. That is more than most people get, and I intend to be extremely annoying about it.
The reckoning at Antrell took a month and went the way Sallow had said it would, which is to say: badly, then boringly, then well.

The badly was the first week. A ring-ship had lost thirty-one spans with four hundred and eleven souls aboard, and there was a bell in scrap, and the Company wanted a person to be at fault, and the person available was a captain who had written, in his own log, in his own hand, on the night of the crack: Bell-master and third-watch hand engaged in an experimental round below the cloudline. Not ordered by me. Not prevented by me.
Marn had done it deliberately. Sol found that out later. He could have written nothing at all.

The boringly was the next three weeks, and it was Halloway's doing, and Sol had never respected anybody so much in her life. The purser arrived at the commission with the tally, the coal ledgers for eleven years, the pour book from the Foundry, Ottring's sworn statement about melt sixty-two, Dov's arithmetic in fair copy, a lease claim filed by a company nobody had heard of, a mail contract, and two hundred and eleven names.
Names. He had gone down on the Sprat himself and taken them, one at a time, with ages, trades and birthplaces, in his very small neat hand.
"You cannot write nil," he told the commission, "in the presence of a list."
The well was the finding, in Elevenmonth, which nobody read out loud because it ran to forty pages and was mostly about lease boundaries. Its substance was four things:

items: The Lowspire Platform Station was recognised as a working station of the Antrell run, with a mail contract and a licensed pair, the second such licence granted in ninety years.
The Meridian Gull was returned to full service, her probation discharged, with a standing order to call at the station once each crossing.
Captain Ovid Marn was censured for permitting an unauthorised round and commended for the conduct of his ship during the settling, in the same paragraph, which he had framed.

Ysolde Kerrin, of no fixed address, was found to have committed a continuing theft of carry over eleven years, and was fined a sum of money she did not have, and was appointed bell-master of the station she had stolen it for, at a salary from which the fine would be deducted, over a period of four hundred and eleven years.

blocks.c: "They enjoyed that," said Sallow. "Commissions have a sense of humour about once a decade and I am glad I was there for it."

Sol asked Kerrin about it, on the platform, in the spring, with the new iron going up on the north frame and the sound of hammers ringing out for eleven hours a day because there was carry enough now to spend on repair.
"Do you regret it?"
"Which part?"
"Any of it. The bell. The eleven years. Not asking."
Ysolde Kerrin, who was seventy-two and looked it, watched two men swing a stringer into place.
"I regret the interval," she said.
"The interval?"

"Four and one. I had it in eleven days. I chalked it on a door in a locked cupboard on a ship and told nobody, because it was mine and because I was going to need it." She flexed her bad hand. "If I had walked up to the ring gallery in Fourthmonth of seventy-eight and said, Tamsin, the count is wrong, here is the true one — the Gull would have had a part in a hundred more carry for eleven years, and the Company would have been eleven years richer, and when I came asking for a bell for a platform full of people they would have had eleven years of reasons to say yes."
She turned round.

"That is the regret," she said. "Not the theft. The theft was arithmetic. The regret is that I had a true thing and I kept it, and everything that happened afterwards happened in the space where that thing should have been."
Sol thought about that for the rest of the spring, and then for a long time after, and it settled into the shape her life took.

She wrote the interval up. That was the whole of her answer, and it looked like nothing: eleven pages, in plain words, with Dov's figures in an appendix, describing how to find the true interval of any bell by ear and by frame, and how to teach the lean to a hand who cannot feel the tenth. She sent copies to the four ships on the run, to the Bellwrights' Company, to the Foundry, and — because Halloway insisted, and Halloway was right about everything except people — to the commission at Antrell, who filed it.

The Cormorant's bell-master wrote back a letter of four lines that Sol kept in the tally for the rest of her career. It said that they had tried the lean, that it worked, that their coal was down two per cent in a month, and that if Miss Ferrant ever came aboard the Cormorant she would find that nobody there would let her pay for anything ever again.
